extracted.intended_audience: clergy, political writers, and learned men preparing sermons or statesmanlike essays
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing sermons/essays aimed at a learned or influential audience that connect scripture, moral instruction, and political wisdom. Emphasizes audience selection, epistemic caution in exegesis, educational aims, and rhetorical form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target the appropriate class of readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Publications should be directed to their appropriate class of readers (e.g., 'exclusively addressed... to men of decent acquitments... the learned').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide at the outset whether you are addressing a promiscuous/general audience or a specialized/learned one; tailor vocabulary, depth, and the amount of explanatory apparatus (glossary, background) accordingly. If addressing the learned, assume some prior learning and press into deeper issues; if addressing the general public, simplify and adjust tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid worldly compromise in sermons
rubrics_metrics.description: Sermons should exhibit 'the absence of all the usual softenings suggested by worldly prudence, of all compromise between truth and' worldly expediency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the purpose is moral or doctrinal edification, prefer plain, uncompromising statement of truth rather than diluting the message to placate worldly sensibilities; still consider prudence in relation to audience and aim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose between general and specialized address
rubrics_metrics.description: One must choose whether to address a 'promiscuous audience' or an exclusive learned audience, as the mode and content should differ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about intended readership on the title-page or preface; the decision affects tone, formality, examples used, and assumptions about prior knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional vividness can compensate for imperfect form
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'overflow of an earnest mind rather than an orderly premeditated composition' can present feelings and impressions more vividly and may offset defects of form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If rhetoric or structure is less than formally perfect, strong earnestness and vivid feeling can still achieve persuasive effect; however, don't rely on this as a substitute for clarity where it matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate the reader's state of mind for scriptural edification
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective perusal of Scripture for edification requires a 'humble and docile state of mind' and especially the 'practice of prayer' as a necessary condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers and preachers should seek to foster humility, inward sincerity, and devotional readiness in their audience (via exhortation, tone, or preface) because mere intellectual presentation without proper disposition will leave Scripture a 'dead language'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education is more than literacy; form faculties and habits
rubrics_metrics.description: Education does not consist merely in teaching reading and writing; it 'consists in educing the faculties and forming the habits'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy proposals or pedagogical writing should emphasize discipline, habit-formation, and cultivation of intellectual faculties rather than treating literacy alone as sufficient; propose measures that require sacrifice and institutional change beyond basic schooling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely solely on mass schooling reforms (Dr. Bell’s model insufficient)
rubrics_metrics.description: Even excellent mass-instruction schemes (e.g., Dr. Bell's plan) are 'a most dangerous delusion to rely on it as if this of itself formed an efficient national education.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat philanthropic/scale schooling schemes as necessary but insufficient; supplement with more demanding measures (moral formation, elite intellectual reform, structural changes) and warn against complacency that basic literacy equates to education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual reform among the learned to educate the labouring classes
rubrics_metrics.description: An efficient education of the labouring classes requires 'a more manly discipline of the intellect on the part of the learned themselves' — a thorough recasting of the moulds shaping future elites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocate reforms targeted at those who educate and govern (teachers, clergy, elites) so they can transmit not just skills but disciplined intellect and character; argue that elite improvement is a precondition of mass improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious before proposing textual interpolations
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not suspect the genuineness of any important New Testament passage 'without great hesitation' and only when 'the most conclusive evidence from the earliest manuscripts and commentators' supports interpolation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Textual criticism and claims of interpolation must be conservative: avoid conjectural emendation, recognize the potential doctrinal consequences, and require strong manuscript/commentatorial support before publishing doubts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid extremes in scriptural interpretation; aim for reflective inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Two opposite errors exist: (a) reducing scripture to mere moral/truth claims (free-thinking liberal reading), and (b) the positive pole that treats mysteries as off-limits to inquiry; the recommended stance is thoughtful personal inquiry leading to 'a full assurance of understanding' and spiritual intuition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage a middle course in exegesis: neither simplistic moralizing nor blind fideism. Promote humble, earnest, and reflective study that allows reasoned assent culminating in inward conviction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promote knowledge as a sacred duty within religion
rubrics_metrics.description: Scriptures distinguish themselves by their frequent 'recommendation of truth' — knowledge is 'one of our most sacred duties' and the glorified spirit is represented as intuitive beholding of truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Religious writing should valorize the pursuit of knowledge and understanding as integral to faith; instruct readers that faith presupposes informed conviction rather than mere acquiescence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use biblical texts to inform political science
rubrics_metrics.description: The Old Testament (and Scripture in general) can be studied as containing 'the elements of political science' and a 'science of realities' applicable to statesmanship and the ordering of society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing for statesmen or political audiences, draw legitimate lessons and principles from scriptural narratives as living 'germs' of political truth, while justifying analogies and avoiding simplistic literalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not expect inward moral formation from popular periodicals alone
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'inward man' will not thrive on the regimen of circulating libraries and the periodical press; popular literature cannot substitute for serious moral and intellectual cultivation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique reliance on ephemeral press and popular print for forming conscience; recommend deeper, structured forms of instruction and ecclesial or educational institutions for moral formation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral reform requires both communication of knowledge and removal of impediments
rubrics_metrics.description: To remove vice and purify principles the means must be the 'communication of knowledge and the removal of those evils and impedimenta which prevent its reception.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Programs aimed at moral improvement should combine teaching (knowledge transmission) with practical reforms that eliminate structural obstacles (poverty, corrupt institutions) that block reception and application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide explanatory apparatus when reviving ancient philosophy or terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern readers will require a glossary and explanation when ancient philosophical terms have to be re-proclaimed, since 'the very terms of ancient wisdom are worn out'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include glossaries, definitions, and pedagogical preliminaries when using archaic or technical language so the intended readers can follow the argument without being misled by obsolete terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conclude with a concise plain recapitulation
rubrics_metrics.description: It 'doth behove me... to recapitulate in as few and as plain words as possible, the sum and substance of its contents.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: End discourses and essays with a clear, concise summary of main points to aid retention and practical application; prefer plainness in concluding statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate reason and understanding in presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Reason (knowledge of the laws of the whole) and understanding (science of phenomena) are distinct but should culminate together: 'reason... culminates in faith... as its crown.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure arguments to show how particular evidence (understanding) leads into general, integrative insight (reason) and ultimately to convictions compatible with faith; do not present empirical detail isolated from higher principles.
